nodes.name: Terminal Request
nodes.notes: No authentication on the webhook itself: the session cookie is the auth, checked in SQL on every request. n8n's built-in Basic Auth is per-webhook, not per-operator, so it cannot express 'who is scanning'.

nodes.name: Read Request
nodes.notes: Hand-rolled cookie parsing -- n8n has no session primitive.

nodes.name: Load Screen Data
nodes.notes: One call returns whatever the current state's screen needs. Always returns exactly one row: an expired or missing cookie comes back as state='login' rather than as an empty result, so there is no empty-result branch to get wrong.

nodes.name: Render Screen
nodes.notes: Every screen renders here. n8n has no way to share code between Code nodes, so the alternatives were duplicating the page chrome per screen or paying an extra workflow execution for a shared render sub-workflow. See the sticky note.

parameters.content:
### The entire read side of the WMS

Five nodes serve every operator screen: login, menu, receiving (3 sub-states), picking (3 sub-states) and stock lookup.

It stays this small only because the per-screen query dispatch was pushed into `wms.screen_data()` and the per-screen HTML into one Code node. Doing either the n8n-native way — a Switch fanning out to a Postgres node and a Code node per state — would be roughly 20 nodes for the same behaviour, and the page chrome would exist in five copies.

So the canvas is readable, but it no longer tells you what the UI does. That trade-off is the finding, not a shortcut.
